# In Praise of Moss

Consider moss, which almost nobody does.

It covers the north side of the tree you walked past this morning, or maybe it doesn't. The "moss grows on the north side" rule is unreliable. Moss grows wherever it's damp enough and shaded enough, which in a thick forest can be any side at all. That's the first lesson moss offers: it doesn't care about your navigation. It isn't there to help you. It's there because the conditions allowed it, and it will stay as long as they do.

Mosses are among the oldest land plants still living. Their ancestors were crawling out of the water and onto bare rock something like four hundred and fifty million years ago, long before there were trees, flowers, or anything we'd recognize as a forest. They have no true roots, only little threadlike anchors called rhizoids that hold on but don't drink. They have no vascular system, no internal plumbing to lift water from the ground to the leaves. So a moss can never grow tall. It stays low, close to the surface, drinking through its whole body, each leaf often just a single cell thick.

This sounds like a list of deficiencies, and for a long time botanists treated it that way. Mosses were "primitive" plants, an early draft that evolution improved upon with ferns, then conifers, then the glorious flowering plants. But moss is still here, on every continent including Antarctica, in deserts and on rooftops and in the cracks of city sidewalks. A draft that has survived four hundred million years of revisions is not a draft. It's a different answer to the same question.

---

The thing about moss that stops me is what it does when it dries out.

Most plants, when they lose too much water, die. Cells collapse and membranes rupture, and the machinery can't be restarted. Many mosses simply stop. They dry to a brittle brown crisp, their metabolism falls to nearly nothing, and they wait. Days, months, sometimes years. Then rain comes, and within minutes they uncurl. Within hours they're photosynthesizing again, green as if nothing had happened.

In 2014, researchers reported that moss cored from deep in the Antarctic permafrost, moss that had been frozen for over fifteen hundred years, began growing again when it was warmed in a lab. Fifteen centuries. It went dormant when the Roman Empire was fragmenting and woke up in a petri dish in the age of smartphones, and it just resumed.

I find that idea strange to hold in the mind. We tend to think of life as a flame: continuous, fragile, extinguished once and for all. Moss suggests something closer to a song that can be paused. The pattern persists even when the performance stops.

---

Moss is also a world in itself. A single clump can be home to thousands of tiny creatures: mites, springtails, nematodes, rotifers, and tardigrades, the famously indestructible "water bears," which share moss's trick of drying out and waiting. If you've ever seen a photograph of a tardigrade, plump and eight-legged and faintly absurd, it was very likely found in moss. To them, a cushion of moss on a stone is a forest, with canopy and understory, wet seasons and droughts. The scale is what makes it invisible to us. We step over entire ecosystems every day.

There's a kind of humility available there, if you want it. Most of what's happening on this planet is happening at scales we don't naturally notice: too small, too slow, too quiet. The dramatic stuff, the lions and storms and elections, is a thin layer on top of an enormous amount of patient, unglamorous activity.

---

Then there's sphagnum, the peat moss, which deserves its own essay. Sphagnum can hold many times its dry weight in water, thanks to large dead cells in its leaves that act like tiny cisterns. It also acidifies its surroundings, creating the soggy, oxygen-poor conditions of a bog. In those conditions, decay slows almost to a standstill. Dead plant matter piles up instead of rotting, layer on layer, for thousands of years, becoming peat.

Peatlands cover only a small fraction of Earth's land surface, but they store an enormous amount of carbon, by most estimates more than all the world's forests combined. A quiet, spongy, unremarkable-looking moss has been one of the planet's great carbon vaults for millennia.

The same preservative chemistry produced the bog bodies of northern Europe: people who died, or were killed, two thousand years ago and were found with their skin, hair, and even facial expressions intact. Tollund Man, discovered in Denmark in 1950, looks as though he's sleeping. The moss kept him.

And during the First World War, when cotton was scarce, sphagnum was gathered by the ton and sewn into bandages. It was absorbent, it was mildly antiseptic thanks to that acidity, and it was free for the picking on the moors. Volunteers, many of them women and children, combed the hillsides of Scotland, Ireland, and Canada, filling sacks. Somewhere in the history of that war are soldiers who lived because a moss that had been quietly growing on a hillside was wrapped around their wounds.

---

In Japan there's a long tradition of moss gardens, the most famous being Saihō-ji in Kyoto, often called Kokedera, the Moss Temple, where well over a hundred varieties carpet the grounds. What I love about the moss garden as an idea is that you can't really force it. You can clear space, provide shade, keep the ground moist, remove the leaves, but the moss decides. A moss garden is less a thing you build than a collaboration you tend over decades. The gardener's main tools are patience and restraint.

That seems like a good way to approach a lot of things. Not everything worth having can be seized. Some things can only be invited, and then waited for.

---

So here's my small proposal: the next time you're outside and it's rained recently, find some moss. Crouch down. Look closely, closer than feels natural. You'll see that what looked like green fuzz is actually a dense miniature forest of tiny stems and leaves, maybe with little stalks rising up holding spore capsules like lanterns. Touch it and feel how much water it holds.

It was here before the dinosaurs. It'll likely be here after us. It asks for almost nothing, and it gives a surprising amount back. It's worth a minute of your attention.

Most things are, if you get close enough.
